1:
Who the spoiler is gets five answers. John Gill reports that some understand Nebuchadnezzar and others Sennacherib, which he grants is more probable; that a rabbi offers a conditional, Sennacherib for Hezekiah's times but the king of nations of the vision for the Messiah's; and that a later scholar applies it to Antiochus, the whole prophecy to the Maccabees. Gill himself takes it of the Roman antichrist, to whom power was given over all kindreds and tongues, spoiler of men's substance by confiscation, their bodies by imprisonment and death, their families by persecution and other men's souls by false doctrine. John Wesley answers in four words: Sennacherib, who wasted Judah.

The two who describe the chapter as a whole contradict each other. Adam Clarke calls its plan peculiarly elegant and manifestly distinct from what precedes, and marks the transitions: the first verse addressed to the Assyrian, briefly but strongly, on the injustice of his designs; the second introducing the Jews at supplication; the third and fourth God himself threatening that the invader shall become easy prey to those he meant to subdue; the fifth and sixth a chorus acknowledging the mercy and power of God. Charles Ellicott says the opposite: no chapter in the prophet presents so little traceable connection, a thought expressed in a verse or two, then another with nothing to link it on.

Ellicott offers two explanations, preferring the second. It may be the strong emotion that filled the prophet's mind as he looked on his country's coming perils; or, more probably as he thinks, we have rough notes, memoranda for a long discourse afterwards delivered in continuous form. They would be more intelligible printed separately, as a French moralist's fragments are printed, since the verse arrangement gives a fictitious semblance of continuity.

On the occasion Ellicott is precise. The words are addressed to the Assyrian on his second campaign, undertaken as it seemed to the prophet without the slightest provocation: the king of Judah had submitted and paid an enormous indemnity for the first war, and had since taken no aggressive action, so the new invasion was undisguised spoliation and rapacity. For treacherously, he would read rapaciously. On such aggressiveness retribution was sure to come, and in that thought the prophet finds his comfort.

John Calvin hesitates between two enemies, and says so. If the words are expounded of the Babylonians the strain flows easily enough, since having just promised freedom to the prisoners the prophet taunts their conquerors, who needed confirming in a prediction that appeared incredible: they could not think it probable that such vast power would be overthrown, and amidst their distresses might have fainted had the prophet not met them with these exhortations. Yet because it is almost universally agreed that a new discourse begins here, addressed to the Assyrian, he is not unwilling to believe it, and takes the threat as a wonderful revolution overthrowing Nineveh, invincible as it appears, when the Babylonians come to punish that cruelty.

Matthew Henry alone reads the verse morally. The sin is that the enemy spoiled God's people and so broke his treaty; truth and mercy are so sacred, and have so much of God in them, that men who make conscience of neither cannot but be under his wrath, and bloody and deceitful men are the worst of men. The aggravation is that he spoiled those who had never injured him and dealt treacherously with those who had always dealt faithfully, whence the rule that the less provocation we have from men to do a wrong thing, the more provocation we give to God by doing it. The punishment answers exactly: the army destroyed by an angel, the camp plundered by those it preyed on, the Chaldeans revolting, and two of the king's own sons murdering him at his devotions — the righteous God often pays sinners in their own coin.
2:
A change of pronoun divides them. Charles Ellicott keeps it: in the shift from their arm to our salvation we hear the prayer as spoken, the first for the soldiers who were to fight, the second for the non-combatants with the prophet. Adam Clarke removes it: the Syriac, the old paraphrase and the Latin read our arm, an early edition has it in the margin, and since the prophet is praying against the enemies the clause cannot be in their behalf; he adopts it though no manuscript confirms it, quoting his own old English Bible, be thou oure arm in erly. John Wesley smooths it over: the change of persons is frequent in prophetic writing.

Keil and Delitzsch take the arm for the power that shelters God's people, needed daily because the danger is renewed daily. Wesley reads every morning of the morning sacrifice, comprehensively rather than exclusively, the morning put for the whole day. John Calvin marks the order: the promise comes first and the exhortation to prayer follows at once, the prophet breaking off his discourse to make it, so the godly know where to go when they seem deprived of all hope. John Gill hears the church under persecution, pleading no merits of her own but casting herself on God's mercy.

The noise that scatters the nations is identified four ways. Gill reports that the Latin renders it the voice of the angel and that a father of the church names Gabriel, others taking it for the noise made in the air or in the camp. Delitzsch says the indeterminate word produces the impression of something mysterious and terrible, then is explained: the noise comes from God, raising himself judicially above Assyria and thundering as a judge. Clarke changes the word again, reading terrible for multitude on the Greek and Syriac, so the clause becomes from thy terrible voice. Ellicott keeps the received text and hears the crash of a mighty tempest.

Calvin treats the defeat as done, bidding the Jews look on the ruin of a power reckoned invincible as having taken place, and noting the plural, since the Assyrian kingdom was made up of various peoples. On the spoil he grants an alternative he does not take, referring the words to the Jews with the noun read actively, but prefers direct address to the Assyrians, since the sudden turn imparts great vehemence when the prophet taunts the proud adversaries. He raises a question the others do not: whether this denotes the nation's final ruin or only the defeat before Jerusalem, and though almost all commentators take the second he finds it too limited.

The image itself all read alike. Ellicott has the invader who came to spoil find himself spoiled, Jerusalem stripping his camp as locusts strip herbage; Gill reports that most understand it of the Jews entering the camp afterwards; Wesley adds that the treasure had been raked together by spoiling many peoples, and that locusts commissioned by God come with force.

Whose times are stable splits them three ways. Wesley turns the words to the king: thy throne shall be established on the sure foundations of wisdom and justice, thy chief treasure in promoting the fear and worship of God. Calvin agrees: the kingdom will yet be prosperous under a pious reign, against the ruinous aspect it wore under his predecessor, and adds that the overthrow of so great a monarchy shows how highly God values his Church's salvation. Gill prefers an apostrophe to the Messiah and the later times when knowledge of him shall cover the earth. Ellicott takes wisdom and knowledge in the higher sense, against the craft of men, and the fear of the Lord as the true treasure, against the silver and gold the king had been led to trust; Clarke notes only that a Greek translator's copy read thy treasure, not his.
7:
One word opens the passage and none agree on it. Charles Ellicott renders it literally, their lions of God, connecting it with the lion-name given to the city earlier: the lion-like heroes of a lion-like city. Adam Clarke reports three manuscripts with a form meaning lions of God, a title for heroes still used among Arabs and Persians, citing a warrior surnamed the lion of God. John Gill follows rabbis who read it as their angels, taking it of the pastors of the churches, the witnesses who prophesy in sackcloth and are slain. John Calvin notes that ancient versions treated it as a contraction meaning I will appear to them, objecting that the form has no parallel.

Calvin raises a question nobody else asks: whether the prophet relates historically the perplexity to which the Jews were reduced, so as to set off the favour of deliverance, or predicts a calamity still to come so the godly should not be caught unprepared. Ellicott has no such doubt: the ambassadors are the envoys sent to the Assyrian at Lachish, weeping at the hard conditions imposed, whether those recorded or a harder demand for the city's surrender. John Wesley says the representation is made lively so the promised mercy may be magnified, the envoys weeping because they cannot obtain their desires.

The broken treaty is agreed. Ellicott says no traveller dared show himself on the road, and denounces the invader for breaking the treaty, the king having complied without any halt in hostilities. Wesley says the same: he broke faith given for a sum of money and contemned the fortified cities he easily took. Calvin adds the commercial consequence: the roads are shut, none go in or out, and merchandise ceases, as commonly happens when war is declared; and he insists the description is the prophet's own, not the ambassadors reporting on the country.

The mourning of the land is read topographically. Ellicott takes the four named places as types of beauty and fertility, cedars, plain, oaks and copse-wood, all now languishing, and suggests the embassy was sent in autumn, so the prophet saw the symbols of failure in the season itself. Calvin observes that the places are widely distant, almost the farthest boundaries of the holy land, so no part will remain uninjured, each assigned what peculiarly belongs to it. Clarke notes only that the Greek read a different word, giving stripped of their beauty. Gill reads it of a later desolation, the witnesses slain and ministry stopped.

On the rising of God the three converge. Ellicott notes the emphatic iteration of the adverb of time, and says man's necessity was, as ever, God's opportunity: he had waited for this crisis and would at once arise in his might. Calvin finds great force in the particle and the repetition, and insists we observe the time: when the Church appeared utterly ruined, which God declares the most suitable moment for assistance. Gill makes it a change of posture: God had been as one lain down asleep, as if careless of his honour, and now determines to arise.

The two images of destruction are handled soberly. Ellicott takes the chaff and stubble as addressed to the invaders, with a side glance at everyone weaving webs of policy instead of trusting God, scheme and result alike worthless, and reads the breath as the hot panting of rage, suicidal instead of destroying Judah. Clarke prefers a conjecture reading my spirit for your breath, on the old paraphrase. Calvin says the Lord laughs at men who think everything in their power when the slightest expression of his will can restrain them. Keil and Delitzsch take the first simile for the totality of the ruin, nothing left but ashes; Ellicott adds that limekiln and thorn-fed oven agree in that residue, Wesley that they burn as easily as chalk.
13:
The summons to hear is a formal preface. John Calvin says the prophet speaks as one handling a very weighty subject, addressing both eyewitnesses and the most distant nations to whom the report would come, so that God's power should be perceived not by a few at hand but far off. Matthew Henry extends it in time as well as space: distant regions and future ages will hear, from the scripture, as surely as those who stood near; those are very stupid who hear and will not acknowledge his might. Keil and Delitzsch and Charles Ellicott note that the judgment on Assyria is a lesson for Israel too, since there is no respect of persons with God.

Calvin then objects to himself: does the subject need so lofty a preface, merely because wicked men were struck with fear? It does, since it is no ordinary exhibition of divine power when wicked men are roused from indolence to perceive, willing or not, that God is their judge — hardest of all in hypocrites, who imagine God under obligation to them and set aside all prophecies by witty jesting.

Who the sinners in Zion are divides them. John Wesley takes them for the Jews, in the unbelieving condition they were in before deliverance came. Henry finds hypocrites who enjoy Zion's privileges and share Zion's services while their hearts are not right. Adam Clarke reasons from the name: Zion is a type of the Church, all whose members should be holy and given to good works, so sinners in Zion are portentous beings — and yet, he asks, where are they not? John Gill rejects the local reading for formal professors in the reformed churches, having a form of godliness without the power, who will panic when God's judgments fall on antichrist — unless his followers are meant.

The fire is left as fire. Delitzsch says that even for the sinners in Jerusalem there is no abiding before the Just One who has judged Assyria: they must repent or go, since God, so far as his wrath is concerned, is a consuming fire. Ellicott makes the everlasting burnings an aspect of God's righteousness. Clarke thinks the old paraphrase worthy of notice: the ungodly ask who shall dwell in Zion where the Divine Majesty's splendour is like a consuming fire, and who in Jerusalem where the ungodly are delivered into an eternal burning; he adds his old English Bible's everdurynge brennyngis.

The answer is the one place a source is identified: Delitzsch calls it the prophet's variation on two psalms, as a later prophet varies another. Gill agrees these are the prophet's own words replying to the hypocrites. Clarke notes a manuscript variant in the clause about the ears: one who stops them to any proposal of bloodshed. Wesley glosses it: just in all his dealings, refusing counsels that tend to shed innocent blood, abhorring the sight of sin in others and guarding his eyes from occasions of it.

The reward is read at three altitudes. Calvin keeps it moral: God's blessing is ready for the upright, who need not dread that burning, since they shall dwell in greatest safety, whereas of slanderers and robbers who cannot restrain tongue, hands, ears and eyes we need not wonder if God is severe: while he is their judge their own conscience is their executioner. Henry keeps it experimental: divine power keeps the believer safe and faith in that power keeps him easy, and the remembrance of their terror adds to the pleasure of deliverance. Gill takes it eschatologically: the saints dwelling by faith now, the spiritual reign after antichrist's fall, and the saints in heaven, safe from those burnings. Wesley says only that it means out of reach of danger, God furnishing necessaries; Delitzsch observes that over this picture the prophet forgets the sinners in Zion and greets the church to come.
17:
The king seen in his beauty is identified two ways, one voice holding both. Charles Ellicott grants that the words, torn from context, have been not unfitly used of the beatific vision, the old paraphrase giving the Shekinah of the King of Ages; but their primary meaning, he insists, is historical. The king is Hezekiah, no longer in sackcloth but in all the beauty of triumph, and the land very far off is all Israel, against the narrow view of men pent within the walls during the siege. John Gill takes it of the King Messiah, seen by the apostles in the flesh and by believers now through faith. John Wesley takes both in order, first Hezekiah and then Christ.

The three officials of the next verse divide them. Keil and Delitzsch make them Assyrian: the officer who raised the tribute, the one who tested the weight of gold and silver, and the one who drew up the plan of the city. Adam Clarke agrees, giving the counter of towers as the enemy commander who surveyed the fortifications to know where to assault. Ellicott names the same three, noting that a psalm uses the last phrase of the city's defenders. Wesley makes them all Jewish instead: the muster-master who kept the list of soldiers, the receiver who laid out money for the war, and the surveyor of fortifications to repair.

Whether the terror is past or coming is disputed. Delitzsch says the dreadful past is so forced out by the glorious present that they must turn back their thoughts to remember it. Ellicott has the heart recall the evil days as a dream that passed, leaving the thankful joy such recollections bring. Calvin refuses the past tense: some render the verb a preterite, others a future, but believing the prophet warns of distresses still approaching he keeps the future, taking the exclamations that follow as speeches reported dramatically. Gill applies the recollection to a later church remembering the slain witnesses.

On the fierce people the argument turns linguistic. Ellicott says the words answer the question just asked: the Assyrian army, with its barbarous speech, is gone. Calvin reports that some translate the word strong and others impudent, but takes it for fierceness, confirmed by the want of a shared tongue: nothing so excites compassion as the speech by which men explain their distresses; where it is wanting each party is a barbarian to the other, and no more can be got than from wild beasts. Wesley says the people seen with terror near the walls are seen no more; Gill makes the fierce countenance a character of the Papists.

Zion restored draws echoes and a piece of trivia. Ellicott hears an echo of two psalms probably written on that army's destruction, and reads the tent that shall not be removed against the threat of deportation. Delitzsch says the prophet passes into the tone of the same psalm. Calvin prefers the accusative to the vocative, and observes that the restoration is set before our eyes as accomplished though the tense is future, for greater energy of style. Clarke would read thou shalt see with the paraphrase, and records the note marking this verse as the middle of the book.

The river that is not there closes the passage. Gill observes that Jerusalem had no Nile or Euphrates for commerce or defence, God promising to be one instead; Ellicott adds that a city boasting only of the softly going waters of Shiloah receives in the divine presence what those rivers were to Nineveh. Calvin gives the reason: a Church resembling a movable tent outlasts the best founded cities because the Lord is in the midst of her; separated from him it would fall without attack, consisting of men only. Wesley says the same of a contemptible brook; Clarke reads the opening words as the glorious name of Jehovah.
22:
The threefold naming is read as one sentence. Charles Ellicott would drop the supplied verb and take the three iterations of the divine name, each with its own characteristic, as the subject of what follows. John Calvin makes it the definition of a church: God dwells among those who worship him as lawgiver and king, so that they who obey know by experience that he guards their salvation while they who merely glory in his name hope vainly. John Wesley glosses the offices: the judge to plead our cause, the lawgiver as chief governor. John Gill refers all three to Christ.

Keil and Delitzsch stop for a page of rigging. Citing a treatise on the ship in Homer and Hesiod, they describe the cross plank joining the vessel's two sides, with a piece cut out on the rudder side where the mast stands, its foot let into a socket in the keel boards; the mast is kept from falling backwards by stays carried to the bows, and on landing is laid into a hollow in the ship's bottom. If the stays are not drawn tight it may fall backwards and slip out of both sockets — the picture the loosed tackling conveys.

Whose ship it is divides one against four. Delitzsch grants that nearly every commentator takes the verse of Assyria, a proud war vessel crossing the river that encircles Jerusalem, but follows a scholar who gave that up: the feminine address points to Jerusalem itself, and gives the most appropriate sense, since the city at present so powerless and sinful would be entirely changed. Ellicott weighs both and takes Assyria as most in harmony with the context, noting that some critics read the terms of a tent's cords and canvas instead. Adam Clarke has the Assyrians wrecked by a violent storm and the people on the beach gathering the spoil, and reports rabbis who refer the chapter to Hezekiah, others who apply it to the days of the Messiah. Calvin addresses the Assyrians and in them every enemy of the Church, whose confidence is that of men rooted to the earth's centre; having made the Church a fortified place ringed with broad rivers, he makes her enemies ships with no foundation.

That the lame take the prey is noticed as an oddity. Ellicott observes that the lame were commonly excluded from the spoils as incapable of active service, and that here they have their portion. Wesley says the spoils left behind would be so many that enough remained for latecomers. Clarke goes further: the army is so shattered that the Jews plunder it without resistance, the most infirm coming in for a share, even the sick throwing aside their infirmities to hasten to the plunder. Clarke also prefers the versions' reading of the mast to the received text, which he finds extremely obscure.

Sickness and pardon are treated as one thing. Clarke says the last line is parallel to the first and says the same otherwise: sickness being a visitation from God and a punishment of sin, forgiveness is equivalent to the removal of a disease, as in the psalm where the second line only varies the first. Ellicott starts the words from the pestilence that attacked the Assyrian army and was probably felt inside the besieged city, so that the prophet, seeing in it the punishment of iniquity, couples health and pardon: healthy because holy was his report of the restored city. Calvin says the second clause explains the first: nothing prevents God's blessings from being enjoyed once our sins are pardoned, and all the miseries that press upon us spring from no other source. Wesley promises not only a temporal deliverance but, infinitely better, the pardon of all their sins; Gill takes the sickness both ways: sin healed by the rising of the sun of righteousness, and persecution brought to an end.
